knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96,
                      fig.retina = 2, message = FALSE)
project <- normalizePath("../../examples/oppeltNPJSystBiolAppl2018")
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = project)
measured <- file.exists(file.path(project, "results", "sensitivities.rds"))
knitr::read_chunk("../../examples/oppeltNPJSystBiolAppl2018/sensitivities.R")
library(dMod2)

A fit, a profile and a mixed-effects model all need the derivatives of the objective in the
parameters. dMod2 computes them exactly: from the sensitivities of the ODE solution, propagated by
the chain rule through every function object of the model, without finite differences. This
chapter shows the four ways to get them, forward, forward over forward, reverse and forward over
reverse, the backends of `odemodel()` and what each costs for the model of the guide. The
numerical methods behind them are the subject of the [cppDE site](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/),
whose articles this chapter links. The code is `sensitivities.R` of the project.

## Forward sensitivities

The states $x(t)$ of an ODE $\dot x = f(x, \theta)$ with $x(t_0) = x_0(\theta)$ depend on the
parameters $\theta$. Their sensitivities $S = \partial x / \partial \theta$, one column per
parameter, follow from differentiating the ODE:

$$\dot S = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, S + \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}, \qquad
  S(t_0) = \frac{\partial x_0}{\partial \theta}.$$

For $n_x$ states and $n_\theta$ parameters these are $n_x n_\theta$ further equations, so the cost
of a solve grows with the number of parameters. cppDE does not write them out: the generated code
evaluates $f$ on dual numbers, each state value with one tangent per parameter, and the integrator
steps states and tangents together. The step-size control includes the tangents (`sensErrCon`),
so that the sensitivities are as accurate as the states
([forward sensitivities](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-forward.html)). An event
that sets a state passes the tangents through the saltation matrix of the jump
([events](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-events.html)).

The observables $y = g(x, \theta)$ have the sensitivities
$\partial y / \partial \theta = g_x S + g_\theta$, and every further function object of the chain
`g*x*p` multiplies by its Jacobian. For the objective $-2 \log L = \sum_i r_i^2 + \dots$ with the
weighted residuals $r_i = (y_i - f_i(\theta)) / \sigma_i$ of the data points $y_i$, the Jacobian
$J = \partial r / \partial \theta$ gives the gradient $2 J^\top r$ and the Gauss-Newton Hessian
$2 J^\top J$, both from first-order sensitivities. The exact Hessian adds
$2 \sum_i r_i\, \nabla^2 r_i$, which needs second derivatives. It matters where the residuals are
large or the model is far from linear in its parameters, and for the terms of an error model
whatever the residuals.

## Forward over forward

The second derivatives of the solution follow from differentiating the sensitivity equations once
more: one equation per state and pair of parameters, $n_x n_\theta (n_\theta + 1) / 2$ in all. dMod2
builds them with `deriv2 = TRUE` in `odemodel()`, `Y()` and `P()`, and an objective called with
`deriv2 = TRUE` and the forward sweep returns the exact Hessian. The number of pairs grows with the
square of the parameters, so this is for small models: the mixed-effects models of
[chapter 7](guide-nlme.html) with a handful of parameters use it, the model of the guide with
`r if (measured) nrow(readRDS(file.path(project, "results", "sensitivities.rds"))$gradients) else "64"`
parameters only once, below, to show what it costs.

## Reverse sweep

The gradient of one scalar, the objective, does not need all sensitivities. The adjoint method
computes it from one backward sweep: with the Lagrange multipliers $\lambda(t)$ of the ODE,

$$\dot\lambda = -\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\top} \lambda
  - \left(\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\top}, \qquad
  \frac{\mathrm{d}(-2 \log L)}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = \int \lambda^\top \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\,
  \mathrm{d}t + \dots,$$

integrated backwards from the last data point, with jumps of $\lambda$ at the measurement times.
cppDE differentiates the integrator itself rather than this continuous adjoint: the *discrete
adjoint* sweeps back through the steps the forward solve took, so the gradient is the exact
derivative of the computed objective. The trajectory of the forward pass is kept at checkpoints and
recomputed between them ([reverse mode](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-reverse.html)).
The cost of the sweep does not depend on the number of parameters: a few times that of the value.

A model is evaluated backwards when every function object of the chain is built with the reverse
direction, `derivMode = c("forward", "reverse")`, and called with `sweep = "reverse"`. `Pimpl()`
passes the sweep through the Jacobian of its root. The value pass runs on the grid of a solve
without sensitivities, and the backward pass sweeps the step grid of that value pass; both run
under the solver `options` alone, while the solves with sensitivities take `optionsSens` merged
over `options`.

In `trust()` the sweep is an entry of each phase:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit <- trust(obj, start,
             phases = list(list(hessianMethod = "gn"),
                           list(hessianMethod = "sr1", sweep = "reverse")))
fit$phaseSweep
```

A phase without `sweep` takes the reverse sweep for `"bfgs"` and `"sr1"` if the objective can be
evaluated backwards at the start, and the forward sweep otherwise. A Gauss-Newton phase always runs
forwards, since $J^\top J$ needs the forward sensitivities; asked for a Gauss-Newton Hessian with
`sweep = "reverse"`, the objective warns and returns none. An `"exact"` phase runs forwards by
default and backwards with `sweep = "reverse"`, where `deriv2 = TRUE` gives the exact Hessian by
forward over reverse. A handover between phases of different sweep evaluates the current iterate
once more. [Chapter 4](guide-optimization.html) compares these Hessian sources on the model of the
guide.

### Accuracy of a reverse gradient

A forward sensitivity is integrated under the error control of the solver; the adjoint of a
backward sweep is not, by default: it follows the step grid of the value pass, whose steps were
chosen for the states. `Xs()` on the cppDE backend controls the sweep through `optionsReverse`;
the solver side is `cppDE::adjointControl()`
([checking the sweep](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-reverse.html)).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
x <- Xs(model, options = list(atol = 1e-8, rtol = 1e-6),
        optionsReverse = list(refine = TRUE, gradtol = 1e-3))
controls(x, "optionsReverse") <- list(refine = FALSE)   # the grid of the value pass again
```

- `refine = TRUE` holds each step of the sweep to the local error test of the CVODES backward
  problem under the absolute and relative tolerances of the solve, and a step that fails it is
  swept again in substeps.
- `gradtol` adds each step's share of the gradient to that test, as its absolute tolerance.

A trust-region method converges with a gradient that is accurate relative to its own size
[@carter1991global; @conn2000trust], so `gradtol` is set as a fraction of the scale of the
gradient.

## Forward over reverse

The exact Hessian without second-order sensitivities: forward tangents, one per parameter, ride on
the backward sweep, which then returns the derivative of the gradient along each tangent, a column
of the Hessian. The cost grows with the number of parameters like a forward solve, but nothing of
order $n_\theta^2$ is integrated or stored
([forward over reverse](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-forward-reverse.html)).
The chain is built with `derivMode = c("forward", "reverse", "forward-reverse")`, and the objective
called with `sweep = "reverse", deriv2 = TRUE` returns the exact Hessian.

The same sweeps give second derivatives along directions only, which FOCEI uses. Its volume term
needs traces $\operatorname{tr}(M\, \partial H_i / \partial \psi)$ with a fixed matrix $M$, and the
joint Hessian applied to a direction of the random effects. The random effects of different groups
never meet in a condition, so the $k$-th random effect of every group shares one tangent $v_k$:
one forward pass along $K$ tangents serves all groups. A backward sweep with the seed $w$ on the
predictions and sigmas of the data rows, and $\dot w_k$ along tangent $k$, returns $J^\top w$ and

$$\sum_r w_r\, \nabla^2 f_r\, v_k + J^\top \dot w_k$$

for every $k$, with $f_r$ the prediction or sigma of row $r$ and $J$ their Jacobian. The rows of
the joint Hessian in the random effects come from one sweep with the gradient of the row loss as
seed and its derivative $L_r J_r v_k$ along tangent $k$, $L_r$ the Hessian of the row loss in
prediction and sigma; they give $\Phi_i^{\eta\eta}$, $\Phi_i^{\eta\psi}$ and the shift of the mode,
$\mathrm{d}\hat\eta / \mathrm{d}\psi = -(\Phi_i^{\eta\eta})^{-1} \Phi_i^{\eta\psi}$. The trace
gradients are linear in $M$: seed $j$ is $2 L_r J_{r,j}$, and along tangent $k$ the derivative of
$L_r$ contracted with $J_{r,j}$ and $J_{r,k}$. Its slice $k$ is $U_{jk}$, and

$$\nabla \operatorname{tr}(M H_i) = \sum_{j,k} M_{jk}\, U_{jk}$$

for every symmetric $M$: $K$ seeds for any number of matrices. The rows of the joint Hessian and the
$K$ trace seeds go back in one sweep, the trailing axis of every cotangent holding $K + 1$ blocks,
a seed and its derivatives along the tangents each. [Chapter 7](guide-nlme.html) describes the
volume term itself.

## Backends

`odemodel(backend = )` chooses the solver. The function objects above it are the same for all
three, and `Xs()` dispatches on the class of the model.

| backend | solver | forward | forward over forward | reverse | forward over reverse | use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `"cppDE"` (default) | generated C++, BDF/NDF, Adams, Rosenbrock, Tsitouras | dual numbers | `deriv2 = TRUE` | discrete adjoint | yes | every model |
| `"Sundials"` | SUNDIALS CVODES through `cppDE::cvode()` | CVODES sensitivities | no | CVODES adjoint (ASA) | no | a cross-check against an established solver |
| `"deSolve"` | `lsodes` of deSolve, equations by cOde | sensitivity equations | no | no | no | the models of dMod |

The step methods and their error control are described in
[stepping](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-stepping.html), the CVODES backend in
[CVODES](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-cvode.html), and the timings of cppDE
against CVODES in the [benchmarks](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/benchmarks.html).

## The model of the guide

`sensitivities.R` builds the chain of [chapter 1](guide-model.html) once more, every function
object with all directions, and evaluates the data term at the best fit of
[chapter 4](guide-optimization.html):

```{r reversechain, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !measured}
cat("> Results pending: `results/sensitivities.rds` of the project is written by `sensitivities.R`.\n")
```

```{r, eval = measured}
s <- readRDS("results/sensitivities.rds")
```

The gradient by the reverse sweep agrees with the forward one:

```{r gradients, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, eval = measured}
max(abs(s$gradients$forward - s$gradients$reverse)) / max(abs(s$gradients$forward))
```

a relative deviation of the order of the tolerances of the solve, since the backward sweep runs on
the step grid of the value pass without `refine`.

The cost of one evaluation, the shortest of ten, in seconds:

```{r cost, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, eval = measured}
s$timing
```

The reverse gradient costs a few values, the forward gradient one solve with a tangent per
parameter. The exact Hessian by forward over reverse costs about
`r if (measured) round(s$timing[["forward-reverse"]] / s$timing[["forward"]], 1) else "5"` forward
gradients. Forward over forward is measured once:

```{r forwardforward, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, eval = measured}
c(seconds = s$forwardForward, s$memory)
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = measured}
peakText <- if (s$memory[["forwardForward"]] > s$memory[["before"]] + 0.05) {
  sprintf("raises the peak memory of the process from %.1f to %.1f GB", s$memory[["before"]],
          s$memory[["forwardForward"]])
} else sprintf("leaves the peak memory of the process at %.1f GB", s$memory[["before"]])
```

It takes `r if (measured) round(s$forwardForward / s$timing[["forward-reverse"]]) else "about 20"`
times as long as forward over reverse and `r if (measured) peakText else "needs little memory"`;
for fits of this model it is a check, not a method. Both give the same Hessian, up to the error of
the solver:

```{r hessians, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, eval = measured}
max(abs(s$forwardForwardHessian[rownames(s$exact), colnames(s$exact)] - s$exact)) / max(abs(s$exact))
```

The eigenvalues of the exact Hessian and of the Gauss-Newton Hessian at the best fit:

```{r, fig.height = 3.5, eval = measured}
eig <- data.frame(rank = rep(seq_len(nrow(s$hessians)), 2),
                  value = c(s$hessians$exact, s$hessians$gaussNewton),
                  Hessian = rep(c("exact", "Gauss-Newton"), each = nrow(s$hessians)))
ggplot2::ggplot(eig, ggplot2::aes(rank, value, colour = Hessian)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(trans = scales::pseudo_log_trans(sigma = 1e-3, base = 10),
                              breaks = c(-1e-1, 0, 1e-2, 1, 1e2, 1e4)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "rank", y = "eigenvalue") +
  theme_dMod()
```

The two agree in the large eigenvalues, the directions the data determine well. In the smallest
they differ: the exact Hessian is positive definite, its smallest eigenvalue
`r if (measured) signif(min(s$hessians$exact), 2) else "0.05"`, while the Gauss-Newton Hessian has
the eigenvalue `r if (measured) signif(min(s$hessians$gaussNewton), 2) else "-0.02"`. The flat
directions are where the Hessian sources of [chapter 4](guide-optimization.html) take different
steps.
